documents.name: Placements and pages
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as ApiStories from "./api.canvas";

export const parameters = {
  layout: "padded",
};

<Meta of={ApiStories} name="Guide" parameters={{ layout: "padded" }} />

# Placements and pages

This guide uses the Core API from `@pstdio/workbench`. A View defines content. A placement puts that View in a region
for the lifetime of the shell, a mode, or a page. The workbench renders panel chrome around each placement instance.
Authors do not register panels.

A placement's `item` decides its lifecycle:

- A static item (`kind: "view"`) has one instance and declares a `presence`: `"fixed"` placements always show and
  cannot close, `"open"` placements start open and the user may close them, `"closed"` placements stay hidden until an
  action or the Add panel opens them. A saved user choice wins over `"open"` and `"closed"` on the next visit.
- A resource item uses `kind: "binding"` and `binding: { kinds, view, cardinality, add? }`.
  `cardinality: "one"` rebinds one instance; `"many"` retains independent resource instances.
  It has no initial visibility: nothing shows until an action supplies a resource.

Opening always goes through the shared navigation executor. `workbench.navigation.openPage(...)` navigates to a page,
and `workbench.navigation.openPanel(...)` opens or activates a declared placement.

## Static placement and presence

The View and placement have different ids in this example. The placement declares `presence: "closed"`, so nothing
shows at registration; the module opens it through `navigation.openPanel`. Press the button inside the workbench:
opening the placement again selects its existing `default` instance.

<Canvas of={ApiStories.StaticPlacement} sourceState="none" />

<Source of={ApiStories.StaticPlacement} />

### What each field means

- `views.registerView({ id, title, body })` defines reusable content. Registering a View opens nothing.
- `shellPlacements.registerPlacement({ id, item, region })` declares one shell-owned placement.
- `item.kind: "view"` makes this a static placement with a single instance.
- `item.view` names the registered View to render.
- `item.presence: "closed"` keeps the placement hidden until something opens it. `"open"` would show it right away,
  and `"fixed"` would show it permanently with no close button.
- `region: "main"` selects the region that hosts the instance.
- `navigation.openPanel({ panel: { kind: "shell-placement", id } })` opens the placement through the shared executor.
  Opening an already-open static placement activates the existing instance instead of adding a tab.

## Resource placement with `cardinality: "many"`

The placement binds one View to the `document` resource kind with `cardinality: "many"`. Preview Alpha, then Preview
Beta: Beta replaces the unpinned Alpha preview. Pin a document before previewing the other one to keep both tabs.
Cardinality controls only how instances map to resources. It does not control initial visibility (a resource placement
always starts empty) and it does not control closability (resource tabs are always closable).

<Canvas of={ApiStories.ResourceTabs} sourceState="none" />

<Source of={ApiStories.ResourceTabs} />

### What each field means

- `item.kind: "binding"` makes this placement resource-bound: each opened resource becomes one instance.
- `item.binding.kinds` lists the resource kinds this placement accepts.
- `item.binding.cardinality: "many"` keeps one instance per resource identity. Opening the same resource again selects its
  existing tab instead of duplicating it.
- `openPlacement({ placementId, resource, open })` supplies the resource that creates or selects an instance.
- `open: "preview"` creates a replaceable tab; the next preview replaces it. `open: "pin"` keeps the tab while other
  resources open. The open intent applies only to `"many"` placements.
- `title` labels the instance tab; without it the tab uses the resource label.

## Resource placement with `cardinality: "one"`

The inspector declares `cardinality: "one"`. Open main, then release: the placement keeps one instance and rebinds it
to the newest resource. Use `"one"` for inspectors and detail panels that always follow the latest selection.

<Canvas of={ApiStories.ResourceRebind} sourceState="none" />

<Source of={ApiStories.ResourceRebind} />

### What each field means

- `item.binding.cardinality: "one"` keeps a single instance. Opening resource B while A is open rebinds the same instance to
  B; no second tab appears.
- Open intent (`"preview"` and `"pin"`) is not accepted here because there is never more than one tab.
- Everything else matches the `"many"` example: the placement starts empty, and its one instance closes like any
  resource tab. Cardinality never changes initial visibility or closability.

## Tab presentation

A tab may replace its View icon with a dynamic status indicator. The workbench renders the indicator as the one leading
glyph instead of showing the indicator and View icon together.

<Canvas of={ApiStories.TabPresentation} sourceState="none" />

<Source of={ApiStories.TabPresentation} />

### What each field means

- `tab.query` returns the current tab snapshot: an optional label, icon, indicator, and menu.
- `tab.refreshEvents` lists the events that invalidate the snapshot and re-run the query.
- `indicator` supplies a leading status glyph with an optional color and accessible label.

## Page composition

A page declares its Main content through `main` and additional panels through `slots`. Navigating to another page replaces that placement set in one
operation. Mode-owned placements remain only when the target page uses that mode.

This example begins on the Session page. Its action navigates to Lab. The Lab page replaces the Session content
instead of opening beside it.

<Canvas of={ApiStories.PageReplacement} sourceState="none" />

<Source of={ApiStories.PageReplacement} />

### What each field means

- `pages.registerPage({ id, ref, path, modeId, resource?, main, slots })` declares a routed page.
- `resource: { kinds }` constrains the route independently of its presentation.
- `main: { kind: "view", view, cardinality }` renders routed content. `"many"` requires a resource-bound page.
- `main: { kind: "panels", empty }` renders peer Main panels and an empty-state view when none are open.
- `slots` contains additional panels. Each uses `item: { kind: "view", view, presence }` or `item: { kind: "binding", binding: { kinds, view, cardinality, add? } }`.
- `navigation.openPage({ page, resource? })` selects the page's mode, commits one canonical location, updates URL and
  history once, and reconciles the page placements in one operation.

import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="0. Empty workbench" />

# 0. Create a workbench

This guide is for host application developers. It uses the Core API from `@pstdio/workbench`.

`createWorkbench()` creates the platform services. `Workbench` renders those services. An empty workbench has no
panels because the host and extensions have not contributed anything yet.

Create one workbench for the lifetime of the host view. Render it inside `WorkbenchThemeProvider`.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.EmptyWorkbench} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={onboardingSources.emptyWorkbench} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

- `createWorkbench()` creates one workbench service container. Every registration in the later guides goes through
  this container.
- The example calls it once at module scope, so the same container lives as long as the host view.
- `WorkbenchThemeProvider` supplies the theme tokens the workbench components need. Render it once, above the shell.
- `Workbench` is the React component that renders the shell layout.
- The `workbench` prop connects the rendered shell to the service container. The shell shows whatever that container
  holds, which is nothing yet.

The next guide adds a placeholder without changing the shell.

documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "./core/placeholder.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="1. Placeholder" />

# 1. Give an empty region a useful state

This is a Core API feature for the host shell. Extensions cannot register placeholders.

A placeholder is shown only while its region has no open panel. Use it for guidance, not for page content. The shell
removes it automatically as soon as a real panel opens in the same region.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.Placeholder} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The outer setup creates and owns the module:

- `createWorkbench()` creates one workbench service container.
- `registerModule(...)` groups registrations under one owner so the workbench can remove them together.
- the module `id` is that owner's stable identity.
- `activate(ctx)` runs once when the host installs the module. `ctx` exposes the Core contribution APIs.

`ctx.views.registerView(...)` defines the placeholder content:

- `id` is the stable View identity. The placeholder refers to this value.
- `title` is the default user-facing label.
- `body.kind: "react"` allows trusted host code to return React.
- `render` creates the content each time the placeholder becomes visible.

`ctx.placeholders.registerPlaceholder(...)` shows that View while a region is empty:

- `id` is the stable identity of this placeholder registration.
- `viewId` names the registered View to render.
- `region` selects the region to watch. The placeholder renders only while `main` has no open panel.

`Stack` and `Text` come from the UI component library. They style the React body and are not part of the placeholder
API.

The View and the placeholder share the id `host.empty-state` here for clarity. They remain separate registrations.

documents.name: 2. Define and place Views
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "./core/views.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="2. Views" />

# 2. Define and place Views

A View defines reusable content. Registering one has no layout side effect: nothing opens until a placement or an
action shows it. A placement decides where a View appears, who owns it, and how it opens and closes.

This example registers two Views and three placements:

1. The **Guide** View fills the Main region. Its placement is `presence: "fixed"`, so it always shows and has no close
   button.
2. The **Instance details** View is registered once and placed twice. The Side Panel placement is `presence: "open"`;
   close it and reopen it from the region's add menu. The Secondary Panel placement is `presence: "closed"`, so it
   waits in the add menu until you open it.

Each visible placement gets its own render input, so the two Instance details panels show different placement
identities even though they share one View.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.Views} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The outer setup creates and owns the module:

- `createWorkbench()` creates one workbench service container.
- `registerModule(...)` groups registrations under one owner so the workbench can remove them together.
- the module `id` is that owner's stable identity.
- `activate(ctx)` runs once when the host installs the module. `ctx` exposes the Core contribution APIs and tracks
  every registration made through them.

`ctx.views.registerView(...)` defines the content:

- `id` is the stable View identity. Placements refer to this value.
- `title` is the default user-facing label. A placement instance may supply a more specific title.
- `body` selects how the workbench renders the View.
- `body.kind: "react"` allows trusted host code to return React. Extensions instead declare native renderer bodies
  such as `tree`, `file`, `kanban`, `dataTable`, and `controls`, or an isolated `webview`.
- `render` creates the content for one visible placement instance.
- `instance` describes that use of the View: the resolved title, resource, placement identity, and instance identity.
  One View rendered in two placements receives two different instances.

`ctx.shellPlacements.registerPlacement(...)` places the content:

- `id` is the stable identity of this shell-owned placement. It is separate from the View id; two placements here
  reuse one View.
- `item.kind: "view"` says this is one static View rather than a resource-bound set of instances.
- `item.view` names the registered View to render.
- `item.presence` sets the initial state: `"fixed"` always shows and cannot close, `"open"` starts open and the user
  may close it, `"closed"` stays hidden until the user or an action opens it. A saved user choice wins over `"open"`
  and `"closed"` on the next visit.
- `region` puts the placement in `main`, `side`, `secondary`, or another shell region.

`Stack`, `Text`, `Code`, `gap`, `p`, and `bg` come from the UI component library. They style the React body and are
not part of the View or placement API.

Keep domain identity in a resource when the same View opens tickets, files, sessions, or other objects. The next guide
shows that form.

documents.name: 4. Let the user open the panel
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "./core/command-menu.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="4. Command and menu" />

# 4. Let the user open the panel

Commands own behavior. The placeholder button, the header menu item, and the command palette all expose the same
commands without copying their handlers. This story uses Core API commands and a host menu; extension commands use
`defineCommand` instead.

Try it in the story:

1. Press **Open command panel** inside the placeholder. The command opens a real panel through the navigation executor
   and the placeholder disappears.
2. Press **Close command panel** in the header to close the panel and reveal the placeholder again. The close command
   is disabled while there is no panel to close.
3. Open the command palette (`Mod+P`, then type `>`), search for "Open command panel" or "Close command panel", and
   run the same commands from there.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.CommandAndMenu} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

`ctx.commands.registerCommand(definition, handler)` declares the behavior:

- `id` is the stable command identity. Menus, keybindings, and navigation actions refer to this value.
- `label` is the user-facing name. The command palette matches against it.
- `category` groups related commands. The palette shows it as a prefix, so "Onboarding: Open command panel" is
  searchable by either part.
- `icon` names the glyph menus and palette rows display.
- `execute` runs the behavior. Opening a placement goes through `ctx.navigation.openPanel(...)`, the same executor
  every other caller uses.
- `isEnabled` gates the command. A disabled command renders greyed out in menus and the palette and cannot run.

`ctx.layout.registerMenuItem(path, item)` exposes a command in one surface:

- `workbenchTopHeaderTrailingMenuPath` places the item in the header's trailing menu.
- `workbenchBreadcrumbLocationMenuPath` places a location action, such as Copy link, in the breadcrumb menu on every
  page. It follows the page resource's own actions. Resource rows in trees do not show it.
- `workbenchCommandPaletteMenuPath` places the item in the command palette. The palette is a menu path like any other
  menu: registering an item there makes the command searchable by label and category. Commands never appear in the
  palette automatically.
- `commandId` names the command the item runs.
- `order` sorts items inside one menu group; `group` selects the group.

The context key wiring keeps the close command honest:

- `ctx.layout.store.subscribeSelector(...)` watches whether the panel is open.
- `ctx.context.set(panelOpenContextKey, open)` publishes that state as a context key.
- `isEnabled` reads the key, so both the header item and the palette row disable together.

A keybinding can run the same command by declaring `action: { kind: "command", commandId }`. Keybindings, menu items,
palette rows, and buttons stay thin: the command is the single owner of the behavior.

documents.name: 5. Add structured navigation
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "./core/tree-renderer.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="5. Tree navigation" />

# 5. Add structured navigation

This story registers the tree through the Core API. Extensions declare the same data through a `tree` view body.

The tree renderer owns hierarchy, expansion, selection, customization, and drag-and-drop. Extensions contribute tree
data instead of rebuilding those interactions.

Press Sessions, Tickets, or Settings. Each row navigates to a registered page and replaces Main. After visiting two
pages, use the workbench Back and Forward buttons to move through the same page history.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.TreeRenderer} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The outer setup prepares the workbench:

- `createWorkbench({ startPage })` creates the service container and names the page to open first.
- `workbench.modes.registerMode(...)` declares the `project` mode. `id` is the mode identity, `label` is its
  user-facing name, and `activate` runs when the mode becomes active. This example needs no activation work.
- `workbench.pageLocations.switchProject(...)` selects the active project. Navigation needs an active project before
  it can commit a page location.
- `pageRef` and `pageTarget` are local helpers. `pageRef` builds the public page reference
  `{ extensionId, kind: "page", id }`. `pageTarget` wraps it in the page NavigationTarget `{ kind: "page", page }`.

`workbench.pages.registerPage(...)` registers one page per navigation row:

- `id` is the stable identity of this page registration.
- `ref` is the public page reference. Navigation targets address the page through this value.
- `title` is the user-facing page name.
- `path` is the URL path segment for the page location.
- `modeId` names the mode that owns the page. Opening the page activates that mode.
- `main: { kind: "view", view, cardinality: "one" }` renders the page content. `slots` contains additional panels.

The tree `body` inside `ctx.views.registerView(...)` supplies the tree data:

- `body.kind: "tree"` asks the built-in tree renderer to draw this View.
- `defaultExpandedSectionIds` lists the section ids that start expanded.
- Optional `getStructure` returns synchronous body sections before content reads begin. Set `loading: true` on pending sections. The host commits the layout before starting content reads; the final body replaces these sections. Extensions use the serializable `body.structure` declaration instead.
- `getHeader`, `getBody`, and `getFooter` each return a list of section groups. Header and footer sections stay
  pinned. Body sections use the available scrolling area. A tree may return more than one group in any of the three
  slots.
- each section has an `id`, an optional `label`, and its `nodes`.
- each node has an `id`, a `label`, an optional `icon` name, and a `target`.
- `target` is a NavigationTarget. Every row here uses a page target. The workbench owns navigation and history, so
  the tree does not need a custom navigation command.
- `getChildren` returns the nested rows under a node. This tree is flat, so it returns an empty list.

`workbench.modePlacements.registerPlacement(...)` places the tree in the Sidenav:

- `id` is the stable identity of this placement registration.
- `ref` is the public placement reference. Navigation targets and keybindings can address the placement through it.
- `modeId` names the mode that owns the placement. The placement appears only while that mode is active.
- `item.kind: "view"` says this is one static View rather than a resource-bound set of instances.
- `item.view` names the registered View to render.
- `item.presence: "fixed"` keeps the tree open while the mode is active. The user cannot close it and the Add panel
  does not offer it.
- `region` puts the placement in the `sidenav` region.
- Sidenav sections are navigation chrome. Content tabs use Main, Side, and Secondary and can move between them.

Owners can restrict drop targets in their tree data. The renderer applies that policy; it does not hard-code
extension or mode ownership rules.

documents.name: 6. Open domain objects as resources
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "./core/resource-panel.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="6. Resource-backed panel" />

# 6. Open domain objects as resources

This story uses the Core API to register a resource kind, a View, and a resource-bound shell placement.

A resource is stable domain identity: a file, ticket, session, or another object a user can open. Passing it to a
placement lets the View load the right data and lets the workbench reuse the right instance. When the module
activates, it opens the Getting started guide as a pinned tab in Main.

Press any **Open** button to add or select a guide tab. The + menu in the Main tab bar now has an **Open another guide**
action. It opens the next closed guide through the same resource placement. The + button disappears when all three
guides are open. Close one tab and the button returns.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.ResourceBackedPanel} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

Each entry in `guides` is a `ResourceRef`, the value that identifies one domain object:

- `type` groups objects of the same kind. The placement accepts only `guide` resources.
- `type` and `id`, together with any extension and project owner, identify this object. Instance reuse follows that identity.
- `id` is the short identity inside the kind.
- `label` is the user-facing name of the object.

The module setup is the same as in the earlier guides: `createWorkbench()` creates the container,
`registerModule(...)` groups the registrations under one owner, and `activate(ctx)` runs once with the Core
contribution APIs.

`ctx.resources.registerKind(...)` declares the resource kind:

- `kind` is the kind identity. It must match the `type` on the resources that open here.
- `label` is the user-facing name of the kind.
- `icon` is the icon name shown for objects of this kind.

`ctx.views.registerView(...)` defines the panel content:

- `id` is the stable View identity. The placement refers to this value.
- `title` is the default label. Each opened instance may carry a more specific title.
- `body.kind: "react"` allows trusted host code to return React.
- `render` receives the render input for one instance. `instance.resource` carries the resource that instance opened,
  so the View reads `label` and its identity from it instead of holding its own state.
- each button calls `openGuide(...)` with a different resource. Reopening a guide selects the tab already bound to its
  identity.

`ctx.commands.registerCommand(...)` gives the placement's + menu a real action:

- `openNextGuideCommandId` identifies the action.
- `nextGuide()` reads the open instances from the layout and finds the first guide that is closed.
- the handler calls `openGuide(...)` with that guide. `isEnabled` returns false when none remain.
- the + menu offers command targets only while their commands are visible and enabled.
- `item.binding.add` links the resource placement to that command. Without an Add action or an accepted active resource, a
  resource placement has nothing to open from the + menu.

`ctx.shellPlacements.registerPlacement(...)` binds the View to the resource kind:

- `id` is the stable identity of this shell-owned placement.
- `item.kind: "binding"` says this placement hosts one instance per opened resource rather than one static View.
- `item.binding.view` names the View that renders each resource instance.
- `item.binding.kinds` lists the kinds this placement accepts.
- `item.binding.cardinality` is required. `"many"` gives each resource identity its own instance, and reopening a resource selects the
  existing tab. `"one"` would keep a single instance and rebind it when another resource opens. Cardinality does not
  control initial visibility or closability: resource placements start empty, and resource tabs are always closable.
- `region` puts the instances in `main`.

`openGuide(...)` calls `ctx.shellPlacements.openPlacement(...)` for one instance:

- `placementId` names the registered placement to open.
- `resource` is the selected `ResourceRef`.
- `title` sets the tab title for this instance.
- `open: "pin"` opens a pinned tab. `"preview"` would open a reusable preview tab instead. Open intent applies only
  to `cardinality: "many"`.

Use page navigation when opening the resource must also establish a routed location.

documents.name: 7. Compose a mode with a page
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "./core/mode-page.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="7. Mode and page contributions" />

# 7. Compose a mode with a page

This is the Core API representation that the validated Extension API compiles into.

A mode contributes context that stays while related pages change. A page contributes content for one location. This
example uses a release project, its tickets, and an active coding session so each owner has visible work to do.

Try these transitions in the story:

1. Start on Project overview. The Sidenav contains **Northstar project** navigation.
   The page's release summary appears in Secondary.
2. Open Tickets. Northstar navigation stays, while Secondary shows the ticket filter.
3. Open the current session. Both project contributions disappear. **Session S-104** navigation and session context
   replace them.
4. Use Back and Forward. The workbench restores the complete mode and page composition for each location.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.ModeContribution} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The outer setup prepares the workbench:

- `createWorkbench({ startPage })` creates the service container and names the page to open first.
- `workbench.modes.registerMode(...)` declares each mode. `id` is the mode identity, `label` is its user-facing name,
  and `activate` runs when the mode becomes active. This example needs no activation work.
- `workbench.pageLocations.switchProject(...)` selects the active project. Navigation needs an active project before
  it can commit a page location.

`registerModeSidenav` contributes the mode-owned navigation:

- the tree View uses `body.kind: "tree"`. `defaultExpandedSectionIds` lists the sections that start expanded.
  `getBody` returns one section with an `id`, a `label`, and its `nodes`. Each node has an `id`, a `label`, and a
  page `target`, the NavigationTarget `{ kind: "page", page }`. The project tree lists Overview and Tickets. The
  session tree lists only the current session. `getChildren` returns an empty list because each tree is flat.
- `workbench.modePlacements.registerPlacement(...)` places the tree. `id` is the registration identity. `ref` is the
  public placement reference. `modeId` names the owning mode, so the placement appears only while that mode is active
  and is removed when the mode changes. `item.kind: "view"` with `item.view` renders one static View.
  `item.presence: "fixed"` keeps it open while the mode is active; the user cannot close it. `region: "sidenav"` places this navigation chrome in the Sidenav.

`registerPage` contributes each page and the Views it renders:

- the main View uses `body.kind: "react"`. Its `render` receives the render input, and `input.workbench` exposes the
  core services. The buttons call `input.workbench.pageLocations.navigate({ kind: "page", page })` to open another
  page and commit one canonical location.
- the tools View is a second React View that renders the page-owned content in Secondary.
- `workbench.pages.registerPage(...)` registers the page. `id` is the registration identity. `ref` is the public page
  reference that navigation targets use. `title` is the page name. `path` is the URL path segment. `modeId` names the
  owning mode, so opening the page also activates that mode.
- `main: { kind: "view", view, cardinality: "one" }` renders the page content.
- `slots` contains the page's Secondary panel with `region: "secondary"` and
  `item: { kind: "view", view, presence: "open" }`. It starts open and the user may close it.
  Saved user choices apply on the next visit.

Shared mode placements keep their identity across pages within the mode. Page panels belong to their page location.
Removing an owning contribution disposes its instances.

This host example registers its Sidenav through the Core API. Extension authors contribute sidebar content through
`navigationItems` and `navigationTrees`, or replace it with `mode.chrome.sidenav`. Extension page slots and mode
placements use Main, Side, and Secondary.

documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "../page-composition/module.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="8. Page composition" />

# 8. Declare the whole page composition

A page declares its Main content through `main` and additional panels through `slots`. This story renders two workbenches so both compositions remain
visible. It does not demonstrate navigation. Story 8 does that.

The first workbench shows Session details in Main, changed files in the Sidenav, and a session inspector in the
full-height Side panel. The second shows Extension Lab in Main, contributions in the Sidenav, and validation output in
the bottom Secondary panel.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.PageComposition} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The outer setup prepares the workbench:

- `createWorkbench({ startPage })` creates the service container and names the page to open first.
- `workbench.modes.registerMode(...)` declares each mode. `id` is the mode identity and `activate` runs when the mode
  becomes active. This example needs no activation work.
- `workbench.pageLocations.switchProject(...)` selects the active project and opens that workbench's start page.

`registerPage(...)` defines three Views for each page:

- the Main View renders the concrete page content.
- the Sidenav View renders page-specific context.
- the auxiliary View renders in the region chosen by that page. Session uses `side`; Extension Lab uses `secondary`.
- each View `id` is stable. Its matching page slot refers to it.
- `title` is the default user-facing label.
- `body.kind: "react"` allows trusted host code to return React.
- `render` receives the render input. `input.workbench` exposes the core services.

`workbench.pages.registerPage(...)` declares each page and its composition:

- `id` is the stable identity of this page registration.
- `ref` is the public page reference `{ extensionId, kind: "page", id }`. Navigation targets address the page through
  this value.
- `title` is the user-facing page name.
- `path` is the URL path segment for the page location.
- `modeId` names the mode that owns the page. Opening a page from another mode switches the mode in the same
  navigation step.
- `main: { kind: "view", view, cardinality: "one" }` renders the Main view.
- `slots` declares the fixed Sidenav panel and the additional panel in `page.auxiliary.region`. Session uses Side; Extension Lab uses Secondary. Each uses the shared `item` contract.

`PageCompositionExample` creates two workbenches with different start pages. It renders both at once so the region
layouts can be compared without changing state. `showNavigation: false` removes the replacement controls from this
story.

Do not open page-owned panels from an activation callback. The page registry is the source of truth, so the runtime can
add and remove the complete page contribution as one unit.

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="9. Page replacement" />

# 9. Replace one page with another

Press **Open Extension Lab**. The Session page's Main, Sidenav, and full-height Side panel disappear. The Extension Lab
page replaces them with Main, Sidenav, and a bottom Secondary panel. Page navigation replaces content and panel
geometry instead of leaving the old page's panels behind.

All callers use the same page-location controller. The controller owns cleanup, mode activation, page composition,
breadcrumbs, and the browser location.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.PageReplacement} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The setup creates the workbench and two modes:

- `createWorkbench({ startPage })` creates one workbench service container. `startPage` names the page to open when a
  project loads without a saved location.
- `sessionPage` and `labPage` are `PageRef` values: `{ extensionId, kind: "page", id }`. A `PageRef` is the typed
  reference that navigation targets use to name a page.
- `modes.registerMode({ id, activate })` declares a mode. `activate` runs when the mode becomes active. These modes need
  no extra setup, so it returns `undefined`.

`views.registerView(...)` defines the page content:

- `id` is the stable View identity. Page slots refer to this value.
- `title` is the default user-facing label.
- `body.kind: "react"` allows trusted host code to return React from `render`.
- `render` receives one render input. `input.workbench` exposes the running workbench services to the content.

The button calls `input.workbench.pageLocations.navigate(...)`:

- the argument is a page navigation target: `{ kind: "page", page }`.
- `navigate` selects the target page's mode, replaces the previous page's placements with the target page's slots,
  commits one canonical location, and updates the URL and history once.

`pages.registerPage(...)` declares each page:

- `id` is the page's stable identity inside the host.
- `ref` is the typed `PageRef` other code uses to open the page.
- `title` is the page label.
- `path` is the page's stable URL segment.
- `modeId` names the mode that owns the page. Opening the page activates this mode.
- `main` renders the Main view. `slots` declares the fixed Sidenav panel and an open panel in Side for Session or Secondary for Extension Lab. Navigation replaces the old page's owned placements together.

`pageLocations.switchProject("canvas")` starts page navigation for one project. It restores that project's saved
location, or opens the start page when nothing is saved.

documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "../api/resource-tabs-example.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="10. Resource cardinality: one and many" />

# 10. Compare one resource with many resource tabs

The Secondary panel starts with three tabs from two resource placements:

- **Inspect main** belongs to a `cardinality: "one"` placement. Press **Inspect release/v0.31**. The inspector keeps one
  tab and rebinds it from `main` to `release/v0.31`.
- **Alpha.md** and **Beta.md** belong to a `cardinality: "many"` placement. Alpha is pinned and Beta is the preview.
  Press **Preview Gamma**. Gamma replaces the Beta preview while Alpha stays open.

Press **Pin Beta** and then preview Gamma. All three documents stay available because each pinned resource identity owns a
tab. Reopening any open resource selects its existing tab instead of making a duplicate.

Press **New document** or the **+** button in Secondary to create another pinned document. Each press creates a new
resource identity, so you can keep adding tabs beyond the three named examples.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.ResourceReuse} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The branches and documents are plain resource values:

- each document is a `ResourceRef`: `{ type, id, label }`.
- `type` groups resources of one type. The resource placement below accepts this kind.
- `type` and `id`, together with any extension and project owner, identify the resource.
- `label` is the user-facing name. The launcher passes it as the tab title.

`inspectBranch` and `openDocument` open resources through `shellPlacements.openPlacement(...)`:

- `placementId` names the registered resource placement to open in.
- `resource` is the document to show.
- `title` sets the tab title for this instance.
- `inspectBranch` omits `open` because its placement has `cardinality: "one"`.
- `openDocument` supplies the open intent. `"preview"` uses the shared preview tab, so
  the next preview replaces it. `"pin"` keeps the tab as a persistent tab.
- the call returns a `PlacementIdentity` that names the created or reused instance.

The first View and placement build the launcher:

- `views.registerView({ id: "guide.documents", ... })` renders the buttons with a `body.kind: "react"` body.
- `shellPlacements.registerPlacement(...)` places it with `item: { kind: "view", view: { kind: "view", id: viewId }, presence: "fixed" }` in
  `region: "main"`. `presence: "fixed"` keeps the launcher always open with no close button.

The document View and placement demonstrate `cardinality: "many"`:

- `views.registerView({ id: "guide.document-view", ... })` renders one document. `instance.resource` carries the
  resource bound to that instance.
- `item.kind: "binding"` makes the placement resource-bound: one instance per opened resource. Resource placements
  start empty; nothing shows until a caller opens a resource.
- `item.binding.kinds: [{ kind: "resource-kind", id: "document" }]` limits which resource kinds the placement accepts.
- `item.binding.cardinality: "many"` creates one tab per pinned resource identity and at most one unpinned preview tab. Reopening a
  resource selects its existing tab.
- `item.binding.add` points to the New document command. The launcher and tab bar run the same command, which creates
  a fresh resource and opens it with `open: "pin"`.
- cardinality controls the instance count only. It does not control initial visibility, and it does not control
  closability: resource tabs are always closable.
- `region: "secondary"` puts the document tabs in the Secondary panel.

The branch View and placement demonstrate `cardinality: "one"`:

- `binding.kinds: [{ kind: "resource-kind", id: "branch" }]` keeps branch resources separate from documents even though both placements use the same
  region.
- `item.binding.cardinality: "one"` keeps one inspector instance. Opening a different branch changes that instance's resource
  and title.
- preview and pin do not apply because this placement can never have a second tab.

The onboarding story passes `showCardinalityComparison` to seed the inspector, a pinned Alpha document, and a Beta
preview. The focused Panels and pages guide renders the same component without the comparison flag so readers can open
the `"many"` placement from an empty state.

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="3. First extension page" />

# 3. Build the first extension page

This extension declares three native file views, places each on a page, and adds sidebar links to open them.
Choose **Pages** or **Views** in the sidebar. The content in Main changes, and the back button returns to the previous page.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.FirstExtensionPage} sourceState="shown" />

## Complete example

The story runs this extension definition. It uses only the public Extension API from `@pstdio/sdk/extensions`.

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

`defineView(...)` creates reusable content:

- `id` is the View's stable local identity. Its `ref` is the typed reference other definitions use.
- `title` is its default user-facing label.
- `body.kind: "file"` asks the host to render a native file view.
- `load` returns the file name and content. A `.md` name selects the Markdown renderer.
- Omitting `save` makes the content read-only.

`definePage(...)` creates the location that owns the View placement:

- `id` creates the page's typed `ref`.
- `title` is the page label.
- `path` is the page's stable URL segment.
- `mode: workbenchModes.project` makes the page available in Project mode.
- `main: { kind: "view", view: view.ref, cardinality: "one" }` renders the matching document in Main.

`defineNavigationItem(...)` creates the action visible inside the workbench:

- `owner` puts the item in Project mode's navigation tree.
- `slot: "content"` places it in the scrolling middle area, below pinned header content and above pinned footer content.
- `group: "Learn"` places it under a visible Learn section.
- `label` and `icon` describe the row.
- `action` is a navigation target. `{ kind: "page", page: page.ref }` opens that page. Page navigation
  replaces the previous page placements instead of appending to them.

Finally, `defineExtension(...)` exports the views, pages, and navigation items as one installable unit. The host loads, validates, and
removes them together. Registering the View alone would show nothing; the page places it, and the navigation item gives
the user a way to reach it.

The Canvas preview supplies a host sidebar that renders Project mode's navigation items. An installed extension uses
the dashboard's sidebar. The sidebar is separate from each page's Main content.

import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "./core/breadcrumbs.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="11. Breadcrumbs" />

# 11. Navigate a full location trail

Breadcrumbs describe the active location and its parents. This story starts at `workbench-core.ts` inside a pull request
review. The header shows five levels: Prompt Studio, Pull requests, #646 Additive pages, Files changed, and the current
file.

The story reached the file by navigating through each parent page. That created real history. Press Back in the header
to return to Files changed. Forward becomes available and returns to the file. Click a breadcrumb ancestor or a button
in Main to create another history entry.

For resource hierarchies, register canonical parent edges and derive the breadcrumb trail from those resources. Avoid a
separate hierarchy that can disagree with navigation.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.Breadcrumbs} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The setup creates the workbench and its page mode:

- `createWorkbench({ startPage })` creates one workbench and names Prompt Studio as its first page.
- `modes.registerMode(...)` registers the Review mode used by all five pages.
- `breadcrumbPages` stores the page identity, label, path, icon, and declared parent.

`workbench.views.registerView(...)` and `workbench.pages.registerPage(...)` build each location:

- the View uses `body.kind: "react"` to render the active location and page buttons.
- `main` renders the page content; `resource` declares its routed resource constraint.
- `parentId` points to the registered parent page. The location controller follows those links to build the breadcrumb
  trail.

The final loop creates the navigation history:

- `switchProject("breadcrumb-story")` opens the root page, Prompt Studio.
- each call to `pageLocations.navigate(...)` opens the next child and pushes a history entry.
- the workbench derives breadcrumbs from the active page and its declared parents. The story never calls
  `breadcrumbs.setItems(...)`.
- Back and Forward replay those saved page locations, so the panel content and breadcrumb trail move together.

documents.name: 12. Choose the correct workbench region
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "../region-map/module.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="12. Workbench regions" />

# 12. Choose the correct workbench region

The area map shows every supported placement region at once. Use it to choose an API target, not as a product layout.
Extension panels use `main`, `secondary`, or `side`. Extensions contribute Sidenav content with navigation items
and trees, or replace it through mode chrome. Host APIs can address additional regions shown here.

The Activity Bar is the narrow strip at the far left. Panel menus are attached to the left and right edges of Main,
Secondary, and Side. They collapse into **Open … menu** buttons when a panel is narrow. Drag a visible menu's resize
handle to change its width or collapse it.

`workbenchRegions` is the canonical region list. `main`, `secondary`, and `side` are panel regions. Each panel owns a
left and a right menu region through `viewMenus.registerViewMenu`. The example attaches both menus to all three panel
Views so you can inspect all six menu regions. The status bar is different: it is not a placement region, so the example
registers a backing View through `workbench.statusBar` instead. The complete area map also lives under **Reference →
Core API → Region map**.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.WorkbenchRegions} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## Side Panel presentation

The Side Panel supports attached, floating, and closed presentations. Modes declare their floating policy. A host
can supply the default:

```tsx
const workbench = createWorkbench({
  initialSidePanelMode: "attached",
  floatingPanels: "hidden",
});
```

`floatingPanels` defaults to `"visible"`. The active mode can override the host default with the same field. Kiln
declares `floatingPanels: "hidden"` on its mode. The controller enforces this setting on transitions, saved state,
and requests. The Float button and bubble launcher use `workbench.sidePanel.canFloat()`.

The presentation is layout state. The `side` region's `visible` flag says whether the panel is open, and its
`presentation` says whether it is attached or floating. Layout persistence saves it with each persistence scope, so
a host that scopes layouts by project or page restores each scope's own choice. A scope without a saved layout uses
`initialSidePanelMode`. When a mode hides floating panels, a floating choice shows attached and comes back when the
mode allows floating again.

Use `workbench.shell.setRegionOpen("side", open)` to hide or reopen the panel. Use
`workbench.shell.setSidePanelPresentation("floating")` to float it when allowed. A forbidden floating request
resolves to `"attached"`. `collapsible: false` prevents dragging closed and still permits explicit hide/show.

Pass `sidePanelBubbleIcon` to the React host to choose a bubble icon. This accepts a React node and defaults to the
chat icon. It changes the icon while keeping the launcher's tooltip, accessible label, and click behavior:

```tsx
import { SlidersHorizontal } from "lucide-react";
import { Workbench } from "@pstdio/workbench/react";

<Workbench workbench={workbench} sidePanelBubbleIcon={<SlidersHorizontal size={20} />} />;
```

The bubble is shown only for closed panels that allow detachment. See the Side Panel stories in the Core API reference
for the default icon, a custom icon, and a panel that stays attached.

## What each field means

`createRegionMapModule()` returns one module contribution. `id` is the module's stable identity, and `activate(ctx)`
registers everything through the module context. `RegionMapPlaceholder`, `regionLabels`, `describeSurface`,
`createRegionResource`, `regionResourceKind`, and `regionWidgetId` are local example helpers, not workbench API.

The setup calls:

- `ctx.sidePanel.setMode("attached")` docks the Side region so it is visible. The other modes are `"floating"` and
  `"closed"`.
- `ctx.resources.registerKind({ kind, label, icon })` declares the resource kind the example's region resources use.

The Views and the status bar:

- `ctx.views.registerView({ id, title, body })` defines one View per region. `body.kind: "react"` renders the
  placeholder content.
- `ctx.statusBar.registerItem({ id, viewId, slot })` places a backing View in the status bar. `slot` is `"leading"` or
  `"trailing"`. The status bar has its own registry because it is not a placement region.

The overlay:

- `ctx.overlays.registerOverlay({ id, viewId, config })` declares an overlay backed by a View.
- `config.modal: false` keeps the rest of the workbench interactive while the overlay is open.
- `config.closeOnInteractOutside: false` keeps the overlay open when the user clicks elsewhere.
- `workbench.overlays.openOverlay(id)` opens it. The button in the Main region calls this.

The shell placements:

- `ctx.shellPlacements.registerPlacement({ id, item, region })` places one View in one region. The shell owns these
  placements, so they exist in every mode.
- `item.kind: "view"` says this is one static View rather than a resource-bound set of instances.
- `item.view` names the registered View to render.
- `item.presence` is required and sets the item's presence. `"fixed"` means the item is always open while its owner is
  active; the user cannot close it, and the Add panel does not offer it. `"open"` means the item starts open when the
  owner has no saved state, and the user may close it. `"closed"` means the item stays hidden until the user or an
  action opens it from the Add panel. A saved user choice wins over `"open"` and `"closed"` on the next visit. Every
  placement here uses `"fixed"` so the whole map stays visible.
- `region` names the target region from the canonical `workbenchRegions` list.
- placements carry no size or collapse settings. Region layout policy lives in `regionSettings` on the mode
  (`defineMode({ regionSettings })`) or on the host (`createWorkbench({ regionSettings })`), and the active mode's
  settings win over the host's.

The panel menus:

- `ctx.viewMenus.registerViewMenu({ id, ownerViewId, viewId, side, regionSize })` attaches a menu to one edge of a panel
  View.
- `ownerViewId` names the panel View the menu belongs to. The menu appears wherever that View is placed.
- `viewId` names the View rendered inside the menu.
- `side` is `"left"` or `"right"`.
- `regionSize` sets the menu region's width in pixels. `defaultPx` is the starting width and `minPx` the minimum. This
  field belongs to view menus only; placements have no size field.

documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "../settings/module.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="13. Settings" />

# 13. Add host settings

This Core API example adds settings owned by the host application. A section groups related entries. A panel supplies
either a preference schema, a custom editor, or a collection-backed editor. The example registers all three panel
kinds, then opens the settings overlay on the Appearance panel.

Choose global or project scope based on who owns the value. The host resolves the active scope; the extension should
not copy project identity into its settings UI.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.Settings} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The module declares the data the settings surface renders:

- `ctx.preferences.registerSchema(...)` registers the named preferences the schema panels edit. Each schema entry
  declares the value type, allowed choices, default, and scope.
- `ctx.settings.registerSection({ id, title, order })` adds one group in the settings tree. `order` sorts sections;
  lower values sort first. Panels join a section through their `section` field.

`ctx.settings.registerPanel(...)` adds one settings page. The `kind` field selects how it renders:

- `kind: "schema"` auto-generates controls from registered preferences. `preferences` lists each entry as a
  preference `name` plus a user-facing `label`.
- `kind: "view"` renders a registered View instead of generated controls. `viewId` names that View. Use it only when
  the shared controls cannot represent the setting.
- `kind: "collection"` renders one tree node per item and opens an item editor View when the user selects a node.

Fields shared by every panel kind:

- `id` is the stable panel identity inside the settings surface.
- `title` is the label shown in the settings tree.
- `section` places the panel under a registered section.
- `scope` says who owns the values: `"global"` values follow the user, `"project"` values belong to one project.
- `icon` names the icon shown next to the panel title.
- `description` is short helper text shown on the panel.
- `save: "apply"` stages edits behind an explicit Save action. Without it, edits save live.

Fields specific to the collection panel:

- `viewId` names the View that edits one selected item.
- `items` returns the current items.
- `itemId` and `itemLabel` derive each tree node's identity and label from an item.
- `groupBy` groups nodes: `key` picks the group for an item, `order` sorts the groups, and `label` names them.
- `actions` adds toolbar actions such as Create. Each action has an `id`, `label`, `icon`, and `run` callback.
- `ctx.settings.refresh()` tells the surface to re-read `items` after data changes.

The item editor View reads its subject from the render input:

- `input.instance.resource?.metadata` carries the `panelId` and `itemId` of the selected collection node.
- `input.workbench.settings.getCollectionItem(panelId, itemId)` returns the matching item.

The host wiring around the panels:

- `createWorkbenchSettingsModule({ resolveScopeId })` activates the unified settings surface: the tree, the
  dispatching panel, and the presenter. `resolveScopeId` maps a scope to a storage key, so project entries appear
  only when a project scope id resolves.
- `ctx.shellPlacements.registerPlacement(...)` with `presence: "fixed"` keeps a launcher View in the `main` region.
  The settings surface is a modal overlay, so the launcher gives the user a way back in after closing it.
- `ctx.commands.executeCommand(WORKBENCH_SETTINGS_OPEN_COMMAND_ID, { panelId })` opens the overlay on one panel.

documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "../preferences/module.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="14. Preference schemas" />

# 14. Declare settings that features can read

A preference is a named setting. A feature reads the setting by name instead of owning a separate settings store.

The schema declares four facts in one place:

- the preference name
- the value type and allowed choices
- the default value
- where the selected value is saved

The settings UI uses that schema to build controls. Feature code reads the selected value from the preference registry.
Both use the same definition, so they cannot disagree about the name, default, or scope.

Try the example in this order:

1. Change **Editor density**. The spacing in **Editor preview** changes.
2. Change **Default open region**. The selected region changes under **New resources open in**.
3. Compare the scope badges. Density follows the user everywhere. The open region belongs only to this project.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.PreferenceSchemas} sourceState="none" />

## When to use this

Use a preference for a choice that must survive after the current panel closes, such as density, a default location, or
a feature option. Component state is still the right place for temporary UI state.

This is the Core API used by an application that embeds the workbench. An extension declares the same kind of setting
under `settings` in `defineExtension`. The host converts that extension definition into a preference schema.

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

Use a custom settings panel only when the shared boolean, number, string, choice, array, and object controls cannot
represent the setting.

## What each field means

The schema declares the contract for each preference:

- `properties` maps each preference name to its schema entry. The name is the stable identity feature code reads.
- `type` is the value type, here `"string"`.
- `enum` lists the allowed choices.
- `default` is the value used before anyone picks one.
- `scope` says where a choice is saved: `"user"` values follow the user everywhere, while `"project"` values belong to
  one Prompt Studio project.
- `description` explains the preference to readers of the schema and to settings UI.

Scope references select which saved value an operation targets:

- `{ scope: "user" }` targets the user's own value.
- `{ scope: "project", scopeId }` targets one project's value. `scopeId` names that project.

The module registers the schema and a panel that uses it:

- `ctx.preferences.registerSchema(...)` publishes the schema so the settings UI and feature code share one
  definition.
- `ctx.views.registerView(...)` defines the demo panel. `body.kind: "react"` lets host code render React, and
  `render` receives the render input for one visible placement.
- `ctx.shellPlacements.registerPlacement(...)` places the View. `item.kind: "view"` places one static View,
  `item.view` names it, `item.presence: "fixed"` keeps it open without a close button, and `region: "main"` picks
  the region.

The panel reads and writes values through the preference registry:

- `input.workbench.preferences.getValue(name, scope)` returns the value saved for that scope, or the schema default.
- `input.workbench.preferences.setValue(name, value, scope)` saves a new value for that scope.
- `useWorkbenchStore(input.workbench.preferences.store, selector)` subscribes to registry state. The example selects
  `state.schemas` to list the registered entries.

documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "../layout-scope/module.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="15. Layout scopes" />

# 15. Persist layouts at the right scope

Users can arrange panels differently per project or workspace. A layout scope selects which persisted arrangement is
active. Changing scope stores the old layout and restores the target layout.

Scope is host state. Extensions contribute placement rules but do not choose persistence keys or restore layouts on
their own.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.LayoutScopes} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The host wires persistence into the workbench:

- `createWorkbench({ layoutPersistence })` accepts the adapter for region layout, including size and visibility.
  The example uses an in-memory map; a real host writes to disk or a database.
- `LayoutPersistenceAdapter` has `getLayout(scope)` and `setLayout(layout, scope)`. The workbench calls them with the
  active scope key, so the adapter stores one layout per scope.

Scopes name one persisted arrangement:

- A `LayoutScope` is a string key such as `"project/demo/mode/tickets/resource/ticket:PS-100"`. The host chooses the
  key format; the workbench only uses it to store and look up state.
- `workbench.layout.setPersistenceScope(scope, options?)` saves the current layout under the old scope and restores
  the layout saved under the new one.
- `carryRegionState: ["sidenav"]` keeps the named regions unchanged across the switch. The example uses it so the
  project-owned Sidenav does not remount while resource scopes rotate.
- `workbench.layout.getPersistenceScope()` returns the active scope key. It lives outside the store, so the example
  mirrors it in local state to drive the button highlight.

The demo controls change state that the scope persists:

- `workbench.layout.setRegionSize("secondary", size)` resizes one region.
- `workbench.shell.setRegionOpen("secondary", open)` hides or reopens the Secondary Panel region.
- `useWorkbenchStore(workbench.layout.store, selector)` subscribes to the live size and visibility values so the
  panel re-renders after each switch.

The rest is the standard module setup:

- `ctx.views.registerView(...)` defines each demo View with a React `body`.
- `ctx.shellPlacements.registerPlacement(...)` places each View. `item.presence: "fixed"` keeps them open, and
  `region` picks `main`, `sidenav`, or `secondary`.
- The story seeds three scopes with different Secondary Panel sizes and open states, so switching shows a visible
  difference.

import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";

<Meta of={ResourceMenuStories} name="Guide" />

# Add actions to resource menus

Resource menus expose commands for one resource kind. The primary slot holds common actions. The context slot holds the
full right-click menu. Both invoke registered commands with the active resource context.

This guide uses the Extension API from `@pstdio/sdk/extensions`. The diagram below shows how two resource kinds resolve
their declared menu slots. An unresolved slot remains visible as a host diagnostic.

<Canvas of={ResourceMenuStories.TwoResourceKinds} sourceState="none" />

## Extension code

<Source code={onboardingSources.resourceMenuSlots} language="tsx" />

Contribute command ids, not React buttons. This keeps visibility rules, keybindings, and command execution consistent.

## Story source

The canvas uses this host-side diagnostic view to show resolved and unresolved slots.

<Source code={diagramSource} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

`defineResourceKind(...)` declares one kind of domain object:

- `id` is the stable kind identity inside the extension.
- `label` is the user-facing name.
- `menuSlots` lists the menu areas this kind owns. Each slot is a named place where commands can appear.

Each menu slot entry:

- `id` names the slot. Commands target the slot by this name.
- `placement` picks the built-in menu area: `"header-primary"` for common header actions, `"header-overflow"` for the
  header's overflow menu, or `"context-menu"` for the right-click menu.
- `access` controls who may contribute. `"owner"` accepts commands only from the extension that declares the kind.
  `"public"` also accepts commands from other extensions.

`defineCommand(...)` declares the action:

- `id` is the stable command identity.
- `title` is the command's user-facing name, shown in surfaces such as the command palette.
- `menus` lists where the command appears. Each entry targets one slot.
- `run(ctx)` executes the command. `ctx.resource` carries the resource the menu was opened on, so the handler knows
  which ticket to act on.

Each menu entry:

- `slot` is the target, built with `resourceMenuSlotRef(kindRef, slotId)`. The helper pairs a resource kind reference
  with one of its slot ids.
- `label` is the text shown in the menu.
- `presentation` picks how the entry renders: a `"button"`, an `"icon-button"`, or a `"menu-item"` row.

`defineExtension({ resourceKinds, commands })` packages the contributions. The host resolves each menu entry against
the declared slots. An entry that targets an unknown slot stays visible as an unresolved diagnostic instead of failing
silently.

import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "../host-terminal-story.tsx?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="16. Host terminal" />

# 16. Connect the native terminal

The workbench owns terminal panels and interaction. The host supplies process operations because only the host can
create a PTY safely. Extensions request a terminal panel without receiving direct process access.

The adapter must forward output events and release sessions when panels close. Keep operating-system details outside
the renderer.

The story opens Terminal 1 at startup. Press **Open another terminal** in Main to create Terminal 2, Terminal 3, and as
many later tabs as you need. The + menu in the Secondary panel runs the same command.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.HostTerminal} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

The host connects a process adapter and activates the terminal module:

- `createScriptedTerminalBridge({ initial })` builds a scripted stand-in for a real PTY bridge. `initial` lists the
  output the terminal shows first. A real host replaces this with an adapter that spawns processes.
- `ctx.terminal.setSessionOpener((request) => ...)` registers the host callback that opens one terminal session. The
  workbench calls it whenever a terminal panel needs a process.
- `createWorkbenchTerminalModule().activate(ctx)` registers the terminal Views and placements. It returns
  disposables the module passes back so deactivation cleans them up.

The demo places a launcher in Main and a plain notes View beside terminals in the Secondary panel:

- the launcher calls `workbench.commands.executeCommand(WORKBENCH_TERMINAL_OPEN_COMMAND_ID)` each time you press its
  button.
- `createWorkbenchTerminalModule()` connects the same command to the terminal placement's Add action, so the Secondary
  panel + menu can also create another terminal.

- `ctx.views.registerView(...)` defines the notes View with a React `body`.
- `ctx.shellPlacements.registerPlacement(...)` places it. `item.kind: "view"` places one static View, `item.view`
  names it, and `region: "secondary"` targets the Secondary Panel region.
- `item.presence: "closed"` keeps the placement hidden until the user or an action opens it. The Add panel offers it.

The story-level setup opens panels and shows persistence:

- `createWorkbench({ layoutPersistence })` creates the workbench, optionally with a layout persistence adapter. The
  adapter has `getLayout(scope)` and `setLayout(layout, scope)`.
- `openWorkbenchTerminal(workbench)` opens Terminal 1 before the story renders.
- each launcher click runs the registered open command, which creates a new terminal resource and tab.
- `workbench.shellPlacements.openPlacement({ placementId })` opens a declared placement by id. The example uses it to
  open the closed notes placement.
- `workbench.layout.setPersistenceScope(scope)` selects which persisted layout is active. The restored story writes a
  layout under one scope, then creates a second workbench on the same scope to show the layout coming back.

documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as OnboardingStories from "./onboarding.canvas";
import source from "./extensions/navigation-levels-extension.ts?raw";

<Meta of={OnboardingStories} name="17. Sidenav levels" />

# 17. Give a page its own Sidenav level

A page can own a `content` navigation tree. Opening that page starts a Sidenav level: the page's sections replace the
mode's body, so the Sidenav shows only what belongs to the page. Header and footer rows stay.

Press Recipes to enter the level. The recipe list replaces the project rows, while Pantry stays in the header. Open a
recipe: its page declares Recipes as its parent, so the level stays open. Press the fixed ← Project button at the
top of the main navigation content to return to the main level. It shows the current mode name and cannot be moved or hidden.
The breadcrumb and browser history also remain available.

<Canvas of={OnboardingStories.SidenavLevels} sourceState="none" />

## Complete example

<Source code={source} language="tsx" />

## What each field means

- `defineNavigationItem({ owner: workbenchModes.project, slot: "header" })` adds a header row to the mode. Header and
  footer rows accumulate from the mode through every open level, so they stay visible in nested levels.
- `defineNavigationItem({ slot: "content", action: { kind: "page", page } })` adds the one main-level row that opens
  the level page.
- `defineNavigationTree({ owner: recipesPage.ref, slot: "content", view })` gives the page its own tree. A page owner
  starts a level; a mode owner adds sections to the main level instead.
- `resourceScope: "project"` reads the tree once for the project. Selecting a recipe keeps its rows visible.
- `parent: recipesPage.ref` on the recipe page keeps the Recipes level open for every recipe. Levels follow the page
  location's parent chain, so a level page opened from another level nests inside it.
- Rows set `resource` as their action subject and `target` as their click destination.

Users can drag rows into the header or footer. Those rows also stay visible inside levels. In the customize menu, users
can hide a level's labeled sections but not its rows. The mode return button stays first in the main navigation content, with the same spacing as other entries.

## Leaving a level

When a child page uses the same resource as its parent, its breadcrumb shows the child page title. The parent keeps the resource label, so the trail names both the resource and the current page.

A level page with no declared parent, such as Recipes, starts the breadcrumb. The host provides a mode return entry
in the navigation panel so users can leave the level.

- Every breadcrumb item that opens a level carries `startsLevel: true`. So does an item whose page belongs to a mode
  that sets `chrome.sidenav`, because that mode also hides the project rows. Hosts can read `items[0].startsLevel`
  when adding their own navigation controls.
- `workbench.pageLocations.navigateToRootLevel()` opens the last location outside every level and every such mode, or
  the start page when there is none. The workbench records that location on every navigation and saves it with the current location, so it
  survives a reload.
- In Prompt Studio, the mode return entry and the active desktop project tab call the same operation. The desktop
  breadcrumb shows only page and resource crumbs. The browser navbar also keeps the project avatar and title as a
  return control.

## Host API

`createLevelNavigation(workbench)` composes one navigation tree from the active mode and every open level. Hosts use
it to fill their navigation view:

- `getSections(slot, signal, onProgress)` returns the sections for `header`, `content`, or `footer`. Pass the tree
  query's `onProgress` callback to show ready sections while slower contributions finish. Results keep their declared order.
- `getReadKey()` changes when the owners or their resources change, so the tree starts a new read.
- `getDefaultExpandedSectionIds()` lists the sections that start expanded.

Outer body rows are returned with `pinnedOnly: true`. The tree view shows them only where users pinned them.
