import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import firstExtensionSource from "../onboarding/extensions/page-extension.ts?raw";
import * as ExtensionApiStories from "./extension-api.canvas";

<Meta of={ExtensionApiStories} name="API reference" />

# Extension API

Use the Extension API to build tools that Prompt Studio can install, validate, enable, and remove. This is the only
workbench authoring API available to first-party and third-party extensions.

| | Extension API |
| --- | --- |
| Audience | Extension developers and agents that build extensions |
| Package | `@pstdio/sdk/extensions` |
| API version | `0.1.0` |
| Code location | An extension package |
| UI runtime | Native host renderer or isolated webview |
| Host access | Validated contributions and declared capabilities |

## Runnable example

This is the complete extension used by the preview. The source panel under the preview shows the same TypeScript that
Canvas runs.

<Canvas of={ExtensionApiStories.RunnableExample} sourceState="shown" />

## Extension entry point

Each contribution has a local id and a typed ref. `defineExtension` collects those contributions. Package identity
comes from `package.json`.

<Source language="tsx" code={firstExtensionSource} />

`defineExtension` accepts arrays named for each contribution type. In this example:

- `views` contains reusable content definitions.
- `pages` contains page locations and their placements.
- `navigationItems` contains user actions that open those locations.

The SDK adds a typed `ref` to every `define...` result. Pass the ref to another contribution instead of copying string
ids. The host adds the extension id when it loads the package.

## Views

`defineView(...)` defines content and does not place or open it.

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | Yes | Stable id inside this extension. The SDK creates `view.ref` from it. |
| `title` | Yes | Default user-facing label. It may be a string or a localizable value. |
| `icon` | No | Design-system icon name used where the host shows View chrome. |
| `body` | Yes | Native View or webview definition. |
| `body.kind` | Yes | Selects `tree`, `file`, `controls`, `dataTable`, `kanban`, or `webview`. |

The remaining `body` fields belong to the selected kind. For example, a tree `body` callback returns sections and
nodes. A file body supplies `load` and optional `save`. A webview body declares its packaged entry and capabilities.
Extensions cannot supply React or register a renderer directly.

## Pages and slots

`definePage(...)` owns a route and its page panels. `resource: { kinds }` constrains an optional routed resource. Main presentation is separate.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `main: { kind: "view", view, cardinality }` | Renders routed content. Multiple instances require a resource-bound page. |
| `main: { kind: "panels", empty }` | Renders peer Main panels and shows the empty view when none are open. |
| `slots` | Additional panels with stable local ids and generated refs such as `page.panels.inspector`. |
| `parent` | Parent page for breadcrumbs and closing the last routed resource view. |

Page slots and mode placements share `item`. Static items use `kind: "view"`, `view`, and `presence`. Resource items use `kind: "binding"` and `binding: { kinds, view, cardinality, add? }`.

`presence` is `fixed`, `open`, or `closed`. Saved user choices win over the initial open or closed state. Fixed panels cannot close. `cardinality: "one"` rebinds one instance; `"many"` retains separate resource instances. A binding opens when given a resource, or on matching page navigation with `openOn: "page-resource"`.

Use `ResourceRef` with `type`, `id`, and optional `label`. URI conversion belongs to routing and persistence adapters. Panel navigation preserves the page resource, URL, and breadcrumbs. Compound targets prepare page and panel steps before committing; commands and links remain standalone actions.

## Mode placements

`definePlacement(...)` attaches a view or resource binding to a mode independently of its pages. It declares `id`, `mode`, `item`, and `region`. Region choices are Main, Side, and Secondary. Page changes within a mode retain shared placement identity. `mountStrategy: "keep-mounted"` preserves local state until the owner leaves.

Modes own `regionSettings` for size, collapsibility, and tab policy. A lone closable panel shows its tab by default. `alwaysShowTabs` explicitly overrides that single-tab policy.

Omitted `chrome` entries retain the host content. Every custom mode gets default host navigation. A view ref replaces that chrome entry; `false` hides it.

Export `qualifyRef(owner, ref)` from a provider contract module for cross-extension use. Local contribution definitions stay local. The helper preserves command types and qualifies nested page-panel refs.

Webviews declare `placement.close` to close themselves with `host.call("placement.close", {})`. The host supplies the calling placement identity and uses the native tab close controller.

## Keybindings

`defineKeybinding(...)` binds a keyboard chord to a navigation action.

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | Yes | Stable id inside the extension. |
| `key` | Yes | Default chord, such as `mod+shift+h`. `mod` is Cmd on macOS and Ctrl elsewhere. |
| `mac`, `linux`, `win` | No | Platform overrides for `key`. |
| `action` | Yes | Any navigation target. A page or panel binds directly; no wrapper command is needed. |
| `when` | No | Context expression that gates the chord. |

## Navigation items

`defineNavigationItem(...)` gives the user a visible way to run an action.

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | Yes | Stable item id inside the extension. |
| `owner` | Yes | Mode or page whose navigation tree receives the item. |
| `slot` | `content` | Pinned `header`, scrolling `content`, or pinned `footer`. |
| `group` | No | Visible section label. Items with the same group are rendered together. |
| `label` | Yes | User-facing item label. |
| `icon` | No | Design-system icon name. |
| `when` | No | Context expression that controls visibility. |
| `action` | Yes | Page, panel, command, link, or compound navigation target. |

## Navigation trees

`defineNavigationTree(...)` adds a tree view to a mode or page navigation slot.

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | Yes | Stable tree id inside the extension. |
| `owner` | Yes | Mode or page that owns the tree. A page-owned `content` tree starts a Sidenav level. |
| `slot` | `content` | Pinned `header`, scrolling `content`, or pinned `footer`. |
| `view` | Yes | Ref of a view with a `tree` body. |
| `resourceScope` | `selection` | `project` reads the tree once per project; `selection` reads it again for each selected resource. |

A Sidenav level replaces the mode's body with the page's sections while that page or a child location is open. Header
and footer rows stay visible from the mode through every open level. A fixed left-arrow button at the bottom of the
header shows the current mode name and returns to the last root-level page. Users can also leave through the
breadcrumb or browser history. See the **17. Sidenav levels** guide for a runnable example.

## UI contributions

| Helper | What it defines |
| --- | --- |
| `defineView` | A webview or a native tree, file, controls, Kanban, or data table view |
| `definePage` | A route, optional resource, Main presentation, and additional panels |
| `defineMode` | A long-lived context with supported workbench regions and region settings |
| `definePlacement` | A mode-owned view or resource binding |
| `defineNavigationItem` | A page, panel, command, link, or compound navigation action |
| `defineKeybinding` | A keyboard chord bound to any navigation target |
| `defineNavigationTree` | A tree view added to a mode or page navigation slot |
| `defineViewMenu` | A view placed in the menu area of another view |
| `defineResourceKind` | Domain identity, resource bindings, and typed menu slots |
| `defineStatusBarItem` | A view placed in the leading or trailing status bar slot |
| `defineSettingsSection` and `defineSettingsPanel` | Extension settings in shared host settings |

## Native view bodies

| `body.kind` | Extension supplies | Prompt Studio supplies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tree` | Sections, nodes, children, and actions | Tree interaction, scrolling, expansion, and customization |
| `file` | Load and optional save callbacks | Text, code, Markdown, and image rendering |
| `controls` | Parameter declarations, values, and mutations | Shared form controls and validation |
| `dataTable` | Columns, rows, and actions | Sorting, paging, selection, and table layout |
| `kanban` | Attributes, rows, statuses, and mutations | Board grouping, filtering, dragging, and card layout |
| `webview` | A packaged UI entry and requested capabilities | Isolation, bridge transport, theme, and capability checks |

Renderer callbacks receive an extension context and structured input. They do not receive the workbench core or a React
render function.

Use the Onboarding guide to build a first page. The Renderers guide covers every `body.kind` with a live preview,
complete extension source, field reference, and concrete use cases.

import { Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as RendererStories from "./renderers.canvas";

<Meta of={RendererStories} name="0. Choose a renderer" />

# Choose a renderer

A View defines content. Its `body.kind` selects how Prompt Studio renders that content. A page or placement then gives
the View a region and a lifetime. Renderer code should not choose its own region or open itself.

```text
extension data or trusted host code
  -> View body
  -> workbench renderer
  -> page or placement instance
```

## Renderer guide

| Body kind | Who can use it | Your code supplies | Good uses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `react` | Core hosts | A React render function | Host chrome, native adapters, trusted application screens |
| `tree` | Core and extensions | Sections, nodes, children, and actions | File trees, navigation, grouped catalogs |
| `controls` | Core and extensions | Form fields, current values, and save callbacks | Properties, settings, filters, creation forms |
| `dataTable` | Core and extensions | Columns, rows, paging, and row actions | Service lists, inventories, audit records |
| `kanban` | Core and extensions | Attributes, rows, statuses, and mutations | Ticket boards, review queues, content pipelines |
| `file` | Core and extensions | Load and optional save callbacks | Markdown, source code, text, images |
| `webview` | Extensions | A packaged UI entry and requested capabilities | Charts, maps, editors, and other custom interaction |

Start with a native renderer. It gives the tool the same keyboard, theme, loading, empty, and error behavior as the
rest of the workbench. Use a webview when none of the native data models fit. Use `react` only for trusted host code.

Each renderer page runs the source shown under its preview.

documents.name: React view
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as RendererStories from "./renderers.canvas";

<Meta of={RendererStories} name="1. React view" />

# React view

`body.kind: "react"` lets a trusted host render a component for each View instance. The callback receives the
resolved `instance` and the `workbench`. The instance carries its resource, title, section, and placement identity.

Use it for host-owned UI that needs direct React composition, such as application chrome, a terminal adapter, or a
native screen that implements platform behavior. Do not use it for installable tools. Extensions cannot send React
through the extension boundary.

<Canvas of={RendererStories.ReactView} sourceState="shown" />

## How it works

1. The host registers a View with a React body.
2. A shell placement, mode placement, or page slot references the View.
3. The workbench calls `render` for each active placement instance.
4. Disposing the owning module removes the View and its placements together.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `render` | Returns React content for one active instance. |
| `instance.resource` | Domain object bound to this use of the View, when present. |
| `instance.config` | Serializable input supplied by the placement. |
| `workbench` | Host commands, navigation, resources, and other Core APIs. |

documents.name: Tree renderer
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as RendererStories from "./renderers.canvas";

<Meta of={RendererStories} name="2. Tree" />

# Tree renderer

`body.kind: "tree"` turns structured sections and nodes into the shared workbench tree. The extension describes data
and actions. Prompt Studio handles indentation, expansion, scrolling, selection, search, drag-and-drop, and pinned
header or footer sections.

Use it for file explorers, project navigation, grouped commands, nested catalogs, or any list whose parent-child
shape matters.

<Canvas of={RendererStories.Tree} sourceState="shown" />

## How it works

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `body` | Returns the main sections and their first node level. |
| `header` and `footer` | Return sections pinned above or below the scrolling body. |
| `children` | Loads children when a node expands. Omit it for a fully loaded tree. |
| `defaultExpandedSectionIds` | Opens named sections on first render. |
| `defaultExpandedNodeIds` | Opens named nodes on first render. |
| `searchable` | Adds the native tree search field. |

A node action is a normal navigation target. It may open a page, open a panel, or run a command. Keep loading and
domain rules in the extension callback. Keep tree interaction in the renderer.

documents.name: Controls renderer
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as RendererStories from "./renderers.canvas";

<Meta of={RendererStories} name="3. Controls" />

# Controls renderer

`body.kind: "controls"` renders JSON-safe field declarations with the shared parameter editor. The extension loads
the fields and current values. It may save each change, apply the full form, reset values, or return a read-only form.

Use it for resource properties, extension settings, filters, small creation forms, and inspector menus. It is a poor
fit for free-form documents or layouts that cannot be described as fields and groups.

<Canvas of={RendererStories.Controls} sourceState="shown" />

## How it works

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `query` | Returns `params`, `groups`, `values`, and optional `readOnly`. |
| `onValueChange` | Saves one changed field and receives the complete current value map. |
| `onApply` | Saves the complete form when the user presses Apply. |
| `onReset` | Restores some or all controls when the user presses Reset. |
| `defaultValues` | Supplies values when `query` does not return them. |
| `emptyTitle`, `emptyDescription` | Explain why no controls are available. |

Omit `onValueChange` for an Apply-style form. Omit both `onValueChange` and `onApply` for read-only properties. The
workbench owns field rendering and validation, so the same declaration works in a panel, menu, or overlay.

documents.name: Data table renderer
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as RendererStories from "./renderers.canvas";

<Meta of={RendererStories} name="4. Data table" />

# Data table renderer

`body.kind: "dataTable"` renders rows against declared columns. The extension owns the query and domain actions.
Prompt Studio owns column layout, sorting, paging, row selection, loading, and empty states.

Use it for service health, inventories, audit records, build lists, or any dense set of records people need to scan
and compare.

<Canvas of={RendererStories.DataTable} sourceState="shown" />

## How it works

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `columns` | Declares stable column ids, labels, descriptions, and optional value renderers. |
| `query` | Returns rows and optional paging details. |
| `selectionMode` | Use `multiple` when actions can operate on several rows. The default is no selection. |
| `selectionActions` | Commands for the current selected row ids. |
| `rowActions` | Commands available for one row. |
| `onRowActivate` | Returns a target to open when the user activates a row. |
| `initialPageSize`, `pageSizeOptions` | Sets the first page size and the choices shown by the workbench. |

Choose a column renderer only when the value needs more than plain text. For example, categorical color works for
health or severity and a color scale works for latency or cost.

documents.name: Kanban renderer
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as RendererStories from "./renderers.canvas";

<Meta of={RendererStories} name="5. Kanban" />

# Kanban renderer

`body.kind: "kanban"` renders rows as a board or list. Attributes define fields that users can group, sort, filter,
and show on cards. A status attribute may point at a shared status provider, so the board and status settings use the
same workflow.

Use it for tickets, approval queues, publishing pipelines, leads, or other work that moves between named stages.

<Canvas of={RendererStories.Kanban} sourceState="shown" />

## How it works

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `attributes` | Declares status, enum, text, date, number, or user fields. |
| `query` | Returns rows for the current renderer settings and filters. |
| `defaultSettings` | Selects board or list mode, grouping, ordering, and visible properties. |
| `onAttributeChange` | Persists a card edit or a move between columns. |
| `onReorder` | Persists ordering within a group. |
| `createRow` | Connects the native create dialog to an extension command. |
| `onRowActivate` | Returns the page or panel target for an opened card. |

The renderer stores each user's view settings. The extension stores domain data. Do not copy board grouping or filter
state into the extension unless it changes the query result.

Card and list property edits appear immediately while `onAttributeChange` saves in the background. Saves run in order.
If a save fails, the renderer restores that edit's saved value, keeps later edits visible, and reports the error.

documents.name: File renderer
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as RendererStories from "./renderers.canvas";

<Meta of={RendererStories} name="6. File" />

# File renderer

`body.kind: "file"` loads a file name and its content. Prompt Studio selects the native Markdown, code, text, or image
view from that name. When the extension supplies `save`, supported text formats become editable and use the shared
dirty-state flow.

Use it for ticket Markdown, generated reports, source files, logs, configuration, and image artifacts.

<Canvas of={RendererStories.File} sourceState="shown" />

## How it works

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `load` | Returns `fileName`, `content`, and optional media metadata for the active resource. |
| `save` | Receives changed text. Omit it for a read-only preview. |
| `refreshEvents` | Reloads the active file after named extension events. |
| `emptyTitle`, `emptyDescription` | Explain why the extension returned no file. |

Keep storage and transport in `load` and `save`. The extension should not choose an editor, track unsaved text, or
implement another save prompt.

documents.name: Webview renderer
documents.content:
import { Canvas, Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as RendererStories from "./renderers.canvas";

<Meta of={RendererStories} name="7. Webview" />

# Webview renderer

`body.kind: "webview"` loads packaged UI in an isolated frame. The extension declares every host capability it needs.
The bridge rejects calls outside that list, and the frame receives the active resource and workbench theme.

Use it for charts, maps, diagrams, rich editors, media tools, or other interaction the native renderers cannot
describe. A webview costs more to build because the extension owns its full UI, accessibility, loading, and error
states.

<Canvas of={RendererStories.Webview} sourceState="shown" />

## How it works

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `entry` | Packaged module created with `packageAsset(path, import.meta.url)`. |
| `capabilities` | Host operations this view may call, such as commands, notifications, or artifact reads. |
| `defineExtensionView` | Defines the guest module and its render function. |
| `createWebviewClient` | Creates the typed bridge client inside the guest. |

Grant only the operations the view calls. Put domain work in extension commands, then let the webview call those
commands through `commands.execute`. This keeps storage and permissions outside the guest UI.

import { Canvas, Meta, Source } from "@pstdio/canvas";
import * as CommandParameterStories from "./command-params-dialog.canvas";
import { commandParamsSources } from "./command-params-dialog-source";

<Meta of={CommandParameterStories} name="Guide" />

# Command parameters

Command parameter schemas describe values that must be collected before a command runs. The workbench renders one
shared dialog from the schema, applies defaults, validates required values, and passes normalized arguments to the
command handler.

Each example now lives on this guide page. Press **Open parameter form** to try it, then compare the schema with the
form the workbench created.

## One number

Use a number parameter when a command needs a count or limit.

<Canvas of={CommandParameterStories.NumberParameter} sourceState="none" />

<Source code={commandParamsSources.number} language="tsx" />

## A real command form

This example combines a template picker with optional long text. The command receives both values in its parameter
object.

<Canvas of={CommandParameterStories.RefineTicket} sourceState="none" />

<Source code={commandParamsSources.refineTicket} language="tsx" />

## Shared control types

Text, selection, multiple selection, number, boolean, and long text fields all come from the same parameter schema.

<Canvas of={CommandParameterStories.EveryControl} sourceState="none" />

<Source code={commandParamsSources.everyControl} language="tsx" />

## Files

The files parameter lets the host upload selected files before the command runs. The command receives file references,
not browser file objects.

<Canvas of={CommandParameterStories.FilesParameter} sourceState="none" />

<Source code={commandParamsSources.files} language="tsx" />

## When a command fails

When the command throws, the dialog stays open and shows the error message in an error box above the actions. The
field values stay, so the user can fix the cause and press **Run** again. Press **Open parameter form**, then **Run**, to
see the planner's "Run attempt" refusing a ticket that waits on another one.

<Canvas of={CommandParameterStories.RunFailed} sourceState="none" />

## Rules

Define parameters on the command. Do not build another form beside the command surface.

Parameters with `resolvedFrom: "resource"` are supplied by the active resource and are not shown to the user. Use host
field renderers only for structured parameter types that the shared editor cannot render.

documents.name: Agent Guide/Component Map
documents.content:
import { Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";

<Meta title="Agent Guide/Component Map" />

# Component Map

Use this map to choose the first component to inspect in the live Canvas catalog.

## Inputs

- Chakra recipe-backed `Button`, `Input`, `Textarea`, `Menu`, `Popover`, `Field`, and `InputGroup` are valid public
  building blocks when their styling comes from `psTheme`.
- `Checkbox`, `Radio`, `Switch`, and `Slider` cover package-owned controls with local behavior or styling beyond Chakra defaults.
- `ParamEditor` and `TagEditor` cover structured editing flows.
- Use icon buttons for compact tool actions and provide accessible labels.

## Navigation and lists

- `Breadcrumb` handles hierarchical page context.
- `Tabs` handles dense in-surface navigation; tab triggers should stay at `xs` density.
- `SearchableMenu` handles filtered action and selection menus.
- `ColumnFileBrowser`, `Sidenav`, `TreeList`, and `ListRow` cover navigable resource structures.
- Use `TreeList` for hierarchical sections and `ListRow` for individual row composition.

## Pannable workspaces

- Use `Canvas` from `@pstdio/ui/canvas` for the dotted background, fixed timeline-style zoom controls, pointer pan, wheel/pinch zoom, and keyboard navigation of a timeline or live-design workspace.
- Canvas callers own their content, camera, and saved layout. Pass the current `zoom`, and update it from `onZoom`. Configure positive `minZoom` and `maxZoom` bounds (defaults 0.25 and 1); every zoom input uses them. Pass the same limits to `zoomCanvas` when applying anchored zoom to a camera. The percentage button resets to 100%, clamped to those bounds.
- `onPan` receives content movement in screen pixels; native-scroll callers negate it. The forwarded ref points to the scroll viewport. Floating controls and the dot pattern stay fixed while content scrolls.
- Mark interactive content or separate drag targets with `data-canvas-control`. This preserves native input while Space-drag and middle-drag still pan over those regions. Keep portals in their native roots.
- Start from `Components/Layout/Canvas` stories for both native scrolling with sticky headers and transformed live previews. Ordinary lists and documents still use `ScrollArea`.
- Use `DependencyTimeline` from `@pstdio/ui/dependency-timeline` for dependency cards arranged in milestone sections and collapsible tracks. It uses `Canvas` and owns card measurement, dependency arrows, sticky headers, and windowed rendering. Supply `TimelineSection`, `TimelineTrack`, and `TimelineItem` data with your own card content, headers, editors, and action callbacks. Keep domain data and saved presentation in the caller. See `Components/Layout/Dependency Timeline`.

## Data display

- `DataTable` handles tabular data.
- `KanbanRenderer` handles switchable board/list data views with filtering, grouping, and ordering.
- `Avatar`, `KanbanRendererCard`, `KanbanRendererList`, `ResourceBadge`, `WorkspaceBadge`, `InfoCard`, and `Activity` cover common data surfaces.
- Use `Foundations/Component Gallery / Composites` for advanced examples before composing `KanbanRenderer`, `ParamEditor`, or `Activity` from scratch.

## Feedback and overlays

- `AlertMessage`, `EmptyState`, `SessionIndicator`, and `Toaster` cover status and feedback.
- `DeleteConfirmationModal`, `Palette`, and `RepoPickerDialog` cover overlay interactions.

## Text and agent UI

- `MarkdownEditor`, `PromptEditor`, `RichMessage`, and collaborative editor stories cover rich-text surfaces.
- `ChatPanel`, `ChatInput`, `ChatMessage`, `ChatPrimitives`, `AttachmentList`, and `ToolInvocationTimeline` cover agent conversation UI.

documents.name: Agent Guide/Foundations
documents.content:
import { Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";

<Meta title="Agent Guide/Foundations" />

# Foundations

Use the `psTheme` Chakra system and package tokens instead of hard-coded visual values.

## Theme and tokens

- Use semantic tokens such as `bg`, `fg`, `fg.muted`, `border.subtle`, and `colorPalette.*`.
- Use package text styles like `paragraph/S/regular`, `label/XS`, and `label/L/medium`.
- Treat Chakra recipe-backed primitives as part of the UI system; import them from `@chakra-ui/react` and change shared
  styling in `packages/ui/src/theme/recipes`.
- Prefer Chakra layout props and local layout components over bespoke CSS.
- Do not change border radius for local preference. Default to `xs` and use the existing recipe radius unless a component
  guide explicitly calls for another radius.
- Preserve theme preference behavior by rendering stories under the configured Canvas decorators.

## Layout defaults

- Use compact, work-focused layouts for product UI.
- Prefer `Stack`, `HStack`, `Flex`, `SimpleGrid`, and package layout helpers for structure.
- Use local components for repeated UI concepts: `EmptyState`, `ListRow`, `TreeList`, `KanbanRenderer`, `Palette`, `Sidenav`, and chat components.
- Keep fixed-format controls stable with explicit sizing, gaps, and responsive constraints.

## Control sizing

- `Button` defaults to `size="sm"` in the theme. Do not restate it unless a local context needs a different density.
- Use `size="xs"` for button-like controls inside tabs, param-editor rows, table/list/tree rows, and other dense row-scoped controls.
- Use `size="2xs"` only for compact icon-only affordances inside rows where the row itself provides the surrounding hit area.

## Visual states

Document meaningful states in stories: default, empty, loading, error, disabled, selected, long content, and dense data. Avoid stories that only demonstrate implementation details.

documents.content:
import { Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";

<Meta title="Agent Guide/Overview" />

# Agent Guide

`@pstdio/ui` is the shared React and Chakra UI package for Prompt Studio surfaces. Treat this Canvas as the source of truth for available components, patterns, design tokens, examples, and usage constraints.

## Agent workflow

1. Inspect the live Canvas examples before writing UI.
2. Use Chakra components directly when `psTheme` provides the recipe or token styling for that primitive.
3. Verify props through Canvas docs, source types, or example stories before using them.
4. Use stories to inspect realistic states, then compose the smallest UI that matches the existing patterns.
5. Add or update colocated stories for user-visible UI changes.

## Component sources

`@pstdio/ui` intentionally uses Chakra as part of the public composition surface. Import recipe-backed primitives such as
`Button`, `Input`, `Textarea`, `Menu`, `Popover`, `Field`, and `InputGroup` from `@chakra-ui/react`; update the local theme
recipes when their shared styling needs to change. Prefer exported `@pstdio/ui` components for custom behavior, richer
product patterns, and package-owned composites.

## Do not guess

Do not invent component props from common design-system conventions. If a prop is not documented or shown in source types, do not use it. Choose a supported prop, compose with Chakra layout primitives, or ask for product direction.

## Where to look

- `Agent Guide/Foundations`: tokens, theme, layout, and styling rules.
- `Agent Guide/Component Map`: component categories and default choices.
- `Agent Guide/Patterns`: higher-level workflows and composed UI.
- `Agent Guide/Preview Authoring`: example structure and coverage rules.
- `Foundations/Component Gallery / Foundations`: lightweight components, tokens, and primitive states.
- `Foundations/Component Gallery / Composites`: advanced component examples for assembled product workflows.

documents.name: Agent Guide/Patterns
documents.content:
import { Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";

<Meta title="Agent Guide/Patterns" />

# Patterns

Patterns are composed UI surfaces. Prefer these when building product workflows instead of assembling primitives from scratch.

Use `Foundations/Component Gallery / Composites` as the quickest visual reference for advanced components before building a new workflow surface.

## Chat

Use `ChatPanel` for full conversation surfaces. It owns the message list, empty/loading states, sticky user-message behavior, workspace hub slot, approval prompt slot, attachment rendering, and input area. Use lower-level chat components only when a host already owns the conversation shell.

Show follow-ups submitted during active work in `queuedFollowUps` immediately. Set `sending: true` until the server accepts the request. Sending rows show their prompt and attachments, and disable editing, removal, and drag actions. Saved rows remain usable while another row is sending. Replace the sending row with the saved request after acceptance; keep failed-send recovery in the conversation.

## Kanban Renderer

Use `KanbanRenderer` when users need list and board views over the same rows. Provide stable row ids, an explicit `storageKey`, typed attributes, and host callbacks for row updates, reordering, creation, and context actions.

Kanban and data tables share saved-view tabs. A custom `CollectionViewsSource` can provide `onReorderViews(ids)` to enable dragging and Alt+Left/Right moves. Save every view ID in its new order and update the source optimistically. Sources without this callback keep their fixed order.

## Tree and row navigation

Use `TreeList` for hierarchical resources with sections, expansion, selection, drag ordering, and context menus. Use `ListRow` when a custom surface needs the same row density, icons, actions, menus, and navigation behavior without a full tree.

## Editors

Use the editor patterns for markdown, prompt input, and rich-message rendering. Keep editor stories deterministic and avoid real network or collaboration backends unless the story explicitly mocks the boundary.

## Diff

Use the diff patterns for changed-file navigation, file summaries, and drawer-based review flows. Prefer documented diff components over building ad hoc file-change cards.

## Dialogs and parameter help

Use `Dialog.Title`, the shared `CloseButton`, and `Dialog.Footer` with grouped actions for creation dialogs.
The workbench overlay owns its close button; widgets supply the header, body, and footer.
Put parameter explanations in `description`. `ParamEditorLabel` shows a tooltip on hover or keyboard focus of its
info button. Escape uses the shared overlay behavior and can also dismiss a containing dialog. Labels do not add an asterisk; required validation
stays in the form.

Selection dropdowns disable themselves when no enabled option or group change can change the value. A sole unset
option can still be selected. Clearable single selections and multi-selections can still remove their selected value.
Action menus keep an enabled selected action available so it can run again.
Declare icons on options and workspace providers; iconless choices stay iconless. Use `git-commit-horizontal` for
branches, `git-branch` for Git worktrees, and `level-low`, `level-mid`, `level-high`, `level-xhigh` for effort levels.

documents.name: Agent Guide/Preview Authoring
documents.content:
import { Meta } from "@pstdio/canvas";

<Meta title="Agent Guide/Preview Authoring" />

# Preview authoring

Canvas examples are executable documentation and live design references. Keep them beside their components in `*.canvas.tsx` files.

## Useful variants

Start with the default useful state, then common configurations and supported edge states: empty, loading, disabled, selected, long content, and errors. Group related states as variants of one component frame.

## Source contents

- Use realistic, synthetic data and deterministic local fixtures.
- Preserve stable IDs and existing exports when updating examples.
- Use Canvas-owned authoring types with an explicit stable variant ID. Keep props, providers, and deterministic setup beside the example. Critical behavioral assertions live in Playwright tests.
- Avoid tests that assert generated wording or bundled copy.
- Split growing fixtures into nearby source files.

## Metadata and validation

Use concise component and variant descriptions when usage needs more explanation than props and examples provide. Rebuild the Canvas catalog, verify source coverage, and test only critical interaction risks in the isolated browser. A successful initial render does not prove every user flow.

Examples are design fixtures, not test cases. Add Playwright checks only for critical user behavior; avoid cosmetic, prop, viewport, and theme permutations.
